title: High-fidelity two-qubit gates in a 7-qubit register for quantum networks
authors: Margriet van Riggelen, Jiwon Yun, H. Benjamin van Ommen, Tim H. Taminiau
abstract: Quantum networks based on optically active solid-state spins may enable quantum technologies including long-range quantum communication and distributed quantum computing. Network nodes containing multiple high-fidelity qubits can facilitate large-scale fault-tolerant operation. However, the stringent error thresholds remain out of reach for multi-qubit registers. In this work, we demonstrate high-fidelity two-qubit gates in a 7-qubit register, based on nuclear spins coupled to a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond. We analyze crosstalk in highly connected spin systems, develop an efficient optimization procedure, and characterize the gates using gate set tomography. The two-qubit gate fidelities (best: 99.61(5)%, average: 99.18(2)%) demonstrate a multi-qubit register at the threshold for distributed quantum computation. Finally, as an example application, we perform a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) simulation of the ground-state energy of H2 and LiH molecules. These results demonstrate one of the key prerequisites for scalable quantum networks based on solid-state spins.
summary: This research demonstrates high-fidelity two-qubit gates on a multi-spin quantum register using NV centers, achieving fidelities near the threshold required for fault-tolerant computation. These hardware capabilities are then leveraged to successfully simulate molecular ground state energies ($	ext{H}_2$, $	ext{LiH}$) via the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE). The work is significant because it validates a solid-state platform's readiness for complex quantum simulation tasks.
main_problem: The work aims to demonstrate high-fidelity two-qubit gates in a multi-qubit solid-state spin register (up to 7 qubits) necessary for scalable quantum networks, while also applying these capabilities to simulate molecular ground state energies.
main_result: High average two-qubit gate fidelities exceeding $99.18\%$ were achieved, placing the system near the threshold for distributed quantum computation. Furthermore, VQE simulations successfully estimated the ground-state energy of $	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{LiH}$ with chemical accuracy using error mitigation techniques.
method: The research combines experimental characterization (Gate Set Tomography) to measure gate fidelities and systematic crosstalk analysis with quantum algorithm implementation (VQE) utilizing advanced error mitigation like Clifford Fitting.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a solid-state spin system involving an NV electron spin qubit coupled to multiple nuclear spins ($^{13}	ext{C}$ bath). The computational tasks involve simulating molecular Hamiltonians ($	ext{H}_2$, $	ext{LiH}$) using the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) algorithm.
key_observables: Two-qubit gate fidelities (best: $99.61\%$), average two-qubit fidelity ($99.18\%$), ground state energy ($\langle H angle$) estimates for $	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{LiH}$, and Pauli expectation values.
important_parameters: Gate parameters include interpulse delays ($	au$), RF frequencies ($\omega_{	ext{RF}}$), and the number of decoupling pulses ($N$). The target accuracy is chemical accuracy (e.g., $1.6 	ext{ mHa}$ for $	ext{H}_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that systematic optimization procedures can effectively mitigate complex crosstalk mechanisms, and VQE simulations rely on the successful implementation of error mitigation techniques like Clifford Fitting.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate gate control schemes (DDRF), crosstalk diagrams, VQE potential energy landscapes for $	ext{H}_2$ and $	ext{LiH}$ comparing simulation to theory, and circuit depth analysis showing sufficient depth for chemical accuracy in $	ext{LiH}$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating fundamental high-fidelity two-qubit gate operations by analyzing crosstalk mechanisms (using GST) to applying these gates as a testbed for quantum chemistry simulations using VQE, culminating in molecular energy estimations.
why_interesting: This work bridges the gap between foundational solid-state quantum hardware characterization and complex quantum simulation algorithms. For AMO physicists, it provides an experimental roadmap showing how engineered spin systems can tackle chemically relevant many-body problems, while the detailed error analysis is crucial for understanding decoherence in solid-state environments.
